relationships.independentReview: Exact mathematical tasks and taught operations independently compared. Both track prime exponents through powers/products and test whether a constraint on the resulting number forces the same constraint on its factors. The original fixes divisibility of one square by12; the candidate applies a supplied even-exponent theorem to products and also constructs a repairing multiplier.
relationships.originalDerivation: The exponent of 2 in n² must be at least 2 and that of 3 at least 1, so n contains both 2 and 3 and is divisible by 6. The legal witness n=6 makes n² divisible by 12 while n is not. This proves I and III and refutes II, F.
relationships.candidateDerivation: The supplied sum-of-two-squares criterion is even exponents on awkward primes. N² is always N²+0², and multiplying two qualifying numbers adds even exponents. N=M=23 is a counterexample to the reverse assertion because 23² qualifies but each factor does not. Multiplying by the product of awkward primes with odd exponents repairs the parity. Only C is false.

relationships.independentReview: Exact mathematical tasks and taught operations independently compared. Both determine which products and quotients preserve an initial order by tracking multiplier signs. The original permits every real sign and includes squares/cubes; the candidate fixes all inputs negative and compares a chain and two ratios.
relationships.originalDerivation: Cubing preserves strict real order. Squaring fails for x=1,y=−2; multiplication by a negative z reverses order, for instance x=1,y=0,z=−1. Multiplication by z² preserves weak order including z=0. Statements 1 and 4, F.
relationships.candidateDerivation: With c<b<a<0, multiplying b>c by a reverses it and gives ab<ac, proving I. Also b(a+c)>0, proving II. Division of c<a by the negative b reverses it, so c/b>a/b and III is false. I and II only, E.

relationships.independentReview: Exact mathematical tasks and taught operations independently compared. Both expand the square of a sine-plus-cosine expression and use sine squared plus cosine squared equal to one to connect the sum and product. The original then computes a symmetric cube sum; the candidate instead audits an unsquaring step and must retain a negative branch.
relationships.originalDerivation: Let a=sin x,b=cos x. Their sum is 1/2 and a²+b²=1, hence ab=−3/8. The identity a³+b³=(a+b)³−3ab(a+b) gives 1/8+9/16=11/16, E.
relationships.candidateDerivation: The tangent premise ensures cosine is nonzero, so division and subsequent squaring through lines I–IV are valid. Taking a positive square root in V discards the possible negative sum. At θ=225°, tan θ=1 while sin θ+cos θ=−√2. Thus V is the first unsupported line, F.

relationships.independentReview: Exact mathematical tasks and taught operations independently compared. Both ask which height/derivative claims necessarily follow from polynomial monotonicity on an interval, using whole-interval counterexamples for claims not forced. The original additionally tests signed area and a midpoint comparison; the candidate additionally compares second-derivative endpoint values.
relationships.originalDerivation: A differentiable nonincreasing polynomial has derivative at most zero, including endpoint limits. The constant polynomial 1 defeats the strict endpoint/integral claims. On [−1,0], f(x)=x² is nonincreasing but f(−1)=1 exceeds 2f(−1/2)=1/2, defeating the midpoint claim. Only the derivative assertion is necessary, C.
relationships.candidateDerivation: A differentiable increasing function necessarily has nonnegative derivative. But 9−x² on [−3,0] is increasing with decreasing derivative, defeating II, and 3x−x³ on [0,1] has nonnegative first derivative but decreasing second derivative, defeating III. I only, B.

Conversely x² on [−1,2] has an interior stationary point but unequal endpoint values. The endpoint condition is sufficient but not necessary, C.
